summary: Defines a metric for the one-way delay of packets across Internet paths. It was replaced by RFC 7679.

plainLanguage.summary: A precise way to measure how long a message takes to travel in just one direction.

questions: why measure one-way delay instead of round trip
what is poisson sampling in network measurement
how is one way delay calibrated
subtitle: A precise definition of one-way packet delay, how to sample it with Poisson timing, and what to report with the numbers.

tldr.problem: Measuring how long packets take across the Internet needs an exact definition, otherwise results from different tools and sites cannot be compared.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a single-packet delay metric, a Poisson-timed sample of such measurements, and statistics such as the percentile, median and minimum, along with the error sources and reporting rules.

today: RFC 2679 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 7679, so that is the document to read for the current definition.

sections.title: Why One-way Delay
sections.content:
This memo defines a metric for the one-way delay of packets across Internet paths, building on the IPPM Framework (RFC 2330). It is a companion to the packet loss metric in RFC 2680.

Delay matters because some applications work poorly if end-to-end delay is large, erratic variation hurts real-time applications, and larger delay makes it harder for transport protocols to sustain high bandwidth. The minimum value reflects only propagation and transmission delay; values above it indicate congestion.

One-way measurement is preferred over round-trip because forward and reverse paths may differ (asymmetric paths), queueing may differ even on symmetric paths, an application may depend mostly on one direction, and quality-of-service provisioning may differ by direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail may go to Grandma by one road and come back by another. Timing only the trip there tells you about that road alone.

sections.title: The Single Measurement
sections.content:
The singleton metric is Type-P-One-way-Delay, with parameters Src and Dst (IP addresses) and T (a time). Its value is a real number of seconds, or undefined (informally infinite).

The delay is dT if Src sent the first bit of a Type-P packet at wire-time T and Dst received the last bit at wire-time T+dT. If Dst never receives the packet, the delay is undefined. Practical points from the RFC:

  • A methodology must decide when a late packet counts as lost; the 255 second theoretical upper bound on IP packet lifetime is one possible bound.
  • If a packet is duplicated, the first copy to arrive determines the delay.
  • If a fragmented packet is not reassembled, it is deemed lost.

The suggested method is to synchronize the clocks, build a Type-P packet whose padding is randomized to avoid compression effects, timestamp it at the source, timestamp it on arrival, and subtract. Since delays often fall in the 100 usec to 10 msec range, the clocks must be closely synchronized.
sections.plainLanguage: You start a stopwatch when the first bit leaves and stop it when the last bit arrives. If the packet never shows up, the answer is "never".

sections.title: Errors, Calibration and Reporting
sections.content:
Clock problems add uncertainty. The RFC lists four notions: synchronization (how well two clocks agree), accuracy (agreement with UTC), resolution (clock precision) and skew (change over time). Only differences between clocks matter, so accuracy per se does not affect a delay measurement. The total clock-related uncertainty is Esynch(t) + Rsource + Rdest.

A second error source is the gap between wire time and host time, bounded by Hsource and Hdest. Calibration aims to find the systematic and random error of the instruments, and at minimum a bound e so that the reported value is within the true value plus or minus e at least 95 percent of the time. GPS time sources greatly reduce the clock uncertainty, whereas ordinary NTP may only reach several msec.

Results MUST be reported with their context: the exact Type-P, the threshold separating large finite delay from loss, the calibration results (the systematic error SHOULD be removed and the calibration error SHOULD be reported), and, if possible, the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Two clocks that disagree spoil the timing, so you must say how far off they might be. A good scientist always reports how sure they are.

sections.title: Sampling with a Poisson Process
sections.content:
The sample metric, Type-P-One-way-Delay-Poisson-Stream, fixes Src, Dst and Type-P, then chooses measurement times from a pseudo-random Poisson process of average rate lambda between a start time T0 and an end time Tf. The result is a sequence of time and delay pairs, which is empty if no times fall in the range.

Poisson timing is used to avoid self-synchronization and to obtain a statistically unbiased sample. The RFC does not constrain lambda, but warns that too large a rate lets the measurement traffic perturb the network, while too small a rate may miss interesting behavior. Implementations must also handle packets arriving out of order, and the Framework suggests the Anderson-Darling test to verify the quality of the Poisson schedule.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of checking at fixed beats, which could line up with a pattern in the traffic, you pick random moments to take your measurements.

sections.title: Statistics of a Sample
sections.content:
The RFC defines four example statistics. In all of them, undefined delays count as infinitely large.

  • Percentile: the X-th percentile of the dT values. For the sample 100, 110, undefined, 90 and 500 msec, the 50th percentile is 110 msec.
  • Median: differs from the 50th percentile only for an even number of values, where the mean of the two central values is used. For 100, 110, undefined and 90 msec, the median is 105 msec.
  • Minimum: the smallest dT, which is 90 msec in the first example.
  • Inverse percentile: the fraction of dT values less than or equal to a threshold. For a 103 msec threshold in the first example it is 50%.

Each statistic is undefined if the sample is empty.
sections.plainLanguage: After many stopwatch trips you can ask "what was the fastest?", "what was the typical one?" or "how many were quicker than this?".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The measurements can harm the network because they are active and inject packets, so parameters MUST be chosen so that they add only trivial traffic. Too much traffic can skew results and, in extreme cases, cause congestion and denial of service.

The measurements can also be harmed. If routers recognize measurement traffic and treat it differently, results will not reflect user traffic, so methodologies SHOULD reduce the chance that test packets can be told apart from normal traffic. Attackers could inject artificial measurement traffic, and authentication such as digital signatures may be used against that. Privacy concerns are limited, since active measurement releases no existing user data.
sections.plainLanguage: Test packets should be few so they do not cause a traffic jam, and they should look like ordinary ones so nobody gives them special treatment or fakes them.

viz.caption: FOUR NOTIONS OF CLOCK UNCERTAINTY (RFC 2679, SECTION 2.2)

items.title: Synchronization
items.text: How far two clocks agree on the time, for example one 5.4 msec ahead of the other.

items.title: Accuracy
items.text: How far one clock agrees with UTC, for example 27.1 msec behind.

items.title: Resolution
items.text: The precision of a clock, for example ticking only every 10 msec.

items.title: Skew
items.text: How accuracy or synchronization changes with time, for example gaining 1.3 msec per hour.
